column2: There were three Bhimasenas, Brahmins, and two Janamejayas; of the second Riksha, Bhimasena was the son.
From Bhimasena came Pratipa, and from Pratipa, Shantanu, Devapi and Bahlika: three great charioteers.
From Shantanu Bhishma was born in that lineage, best of Brahmins. Now hear the lineage of the royal sage Bahlika, Brahmins.
Bahlika's son was the greatly famed Somadatta; from Somadatta were born Bhuri, Bhurishravas and Shala.
Devapi became a sage, the priest of the gods; Kritaka, son of Chyavana, was beloved of the great-souled one.
Shantanu became king, bearer of the burden of the Kauravas. I shall tell the lineage of Shantanu, famed in the three worlds.
The lord begot the son Devavrata, son of the Ganga, who was famed as Bhishma, grandfather of the Pandavas.
Kali (Satyavati) bore Vichitravirya, Brahmins, Shantanu's beloved son, righteous-souled and faultless.
And from Krishna Dvaipayana, on Vichitravirya's wives, she begot Dhritarashtra, Pandu and Vidura.
Dhritarashtra begot a hundred sons on Gandhari; of them Duryodhana was the eldest, lord of them all.
Pandu's son was Dhananjaya; Subhadra's son was his son (Abhimanyu); Abhimanyu's son was Parikshit, the father of Parikshit's (son).
Parikshit's son on a Kashi princess had two sons: the king Chandrapida and Suryapida, a knower of liberation.
Chandrapida had a hundred excellent-archer sons; the Kshatriya line of Janamejaya was thus renowned on earth.
The eldest of them was in the city called Varanasahvaya (Hastinapura): Satyakarna, mighty-armed, a sacrificer, giver of ample fees.
Satyakarna's heir was the mighty Shvetakarna; childless, the righteous-souled one entered the austerity forest.
By him a Yadava woman, gone to the forest, conceived: Malini, daughter of Sucharu, fair-browed, Grahamalini.
When the embryo was conceived, Shvetakarna, lord of the people, followed the unfailing great departure done before.
Seeing her beloved, Malini, Sucharu's virtuous daughter with lotus eyes, followed behind him in the forest.
On the way the young woman bore a very delicate boy; leaving him there, she followed the king.
Devoted to her husband and fortunate, as Draupadi was of old, the lady... the delicate boy cried on the mountain's back.
Out of compassion clouds appeared for the great-souled boy; of Shravishtha two sons, Paippaladi and Kaushika,
seeing him, compassionate, took him and washed him in water; his two sides, rubbed on a rock, were drenched in blood.
Ajashyama, well composed, by the rubbing of the sides — his two sides became goat-dark by the god's will.
Therefore the two Brahmins gave him the name Ajapārshva; he was raised by the two Brahmins in Remaka's hall.
Remaka's wife took him up for the sake of a son; Rematy's son he became, and the two Brahmins were his ministers.
Their sons and grandsons lived equally long at the same time. This is the Paurava line of the great-souled Pandavas.
Here too this verse was sung by Yayati son of Nahusha, long ago, at the transfer of old age, then pleased and wise:
Without doubt this earth may exist without moon, sun and planets, but never will the earth be without Pauravas.
This Paurava lineage, famed, has been told to you by me; I shall tell of Turvasu, Druhyu, Anu and Yadu.
Turvasu's son was Vahni, and his son Gobhanu; Gobhanu's son was the unconquered king Aishanu.
Aishanu's son was Karandhama, and his son Marutta; another Marutta, son of Avikshit, has been told by me.
That king was childless, a sacrificer, giver of ample fees; the lord of the earth had a daughter named Samyata.
She was given as a fee to the great-souled Samvarta, and he also obtained a faultless Paurava son, Dushyanta.
Thus, by Yayati's curse at the transfer of old age, the Paurava entered Turvasu's line, best of Brahmins.
Dushyanta's heir was the lord of creatures Karuroma; from Karuroma, Ahrida; he had four sons:
Pandya, Kerala, Kala and Chola, kings. Druhyu's son, king, was the king Babhrusetu.
His son Angarasetu is called lord of the Maruts; the mighty one was killed with difficulty in battle by Yauvanashva.
The war was very great, lasting ten months. Angarasetu's heir was the king named Gandhara,
by whose name the great Gandhara country is famed, and the horses born in Gandhara are the best of horses.
Anu's son was Dharma, and his son was Dyuta; from Dyuta was born Vanaduha, and his son Prachetas.
The Anavas Prachetas and Suchetas have been told by me. Yadu had five sons, like sons of gods:
Sahasrada, Payoda, Kroshtu, Nila and Anjika. Sahasrada had three exceedingly righteous heirs:
Haihaya, Haya and the king Venuhaya. Haihaya's son was known as Dharmanetra.
Dharmanetra's son was Karta; his son Sahanja; the city Sahanjani was founded by that king.
Mahishmat's son was the mighty Bhadrashrenya; Bhadrashrenya's heir was the renowned Durdama.
Durdama's wise son was named Kanaka; Kanaka had four heirs famed in the world:
Kritavirya, Kritaujas, Kritadhanva and Kritagni the fourth; from Kritavirya came Arjuna.
He, with a thousand arms, became lord of the seven continents; alone he conquered the earth with a chariot radiant as the sun.
He practised extremely difficult austerity for ten thousand years and propitiated Datta, born of Atri, Kartavirya.
He (Datta) granted him four boons of great radiance; first a thousand arms was asked for, a very great boon;
when he is engaged in unrighteousness, restraint by the good there; having conquered the earth by force, ruling it with dharma only;
having conquered very many battles and slain enemies by thousands, his death in battle at the hands of one superior in the fight.
Of him, as he fought, a thousand arms appeared, Brahmins, through yoga, by illusion, like that of a lord of yogis.
By him this whole earth with seven continents, cities, oceans and towns was conquered by a fierce method.
By that king, it is heard, seven hundred sacrifices were performed by rule in the seven continents, best of sages.
All the sacrifices, best of sages, had fees of a hundred thousand, all had golden sacrificial posts and all golden altars,
all were constantly adorned with gods seated in decorated aerial cars, with Gandharvas and Apsarases.
At whose sacrifice the Gandharva and Narada sang a verse; the learned son of Varidasa was amazed at his greatness:
Surely other kings will not reach the state of Kartavirya in sacrifices, gifts, austerities, valour and learning.
In the seven continents he was seen by men as a yogi roaming the continents with shield, sword, bow and chariot.
No loss of property, no grief, no confusion: through the great king's power, as he protected his people with dharma.
He became the emperor, universal sovereign, partaker of all jewels; he alone was the cattle-keeper and he alone the field-guardian,
he alone was the rain-cloud with rain; through yoga he became Arjuna. With a thousand arms, hard from the bowstring's strike,
he shone with a thousand rays like the sun in autumn. That greatly radiant one at Mahishmati, among humans, (conquered) the Nagas,
defeating Karkotaka's sons, and settled them in that city. The lotus-eyed one in the rainy season, as if playing, turned the ocean's force
against the current with his arms; as he played, the river became tangled, with villages as her garland.
With a thousand moving waves, the Narmada came to him fearfully; while the great ocean was churned by his thousand arms,
out of fear the Brahmins staying in the nether world hid, motionless; the great waves broken to powder, great whales and timingilas moving,
foam-masses tossed by wind, confused with whirlpools — the king set it in motion with his thousand arms,
like Mandara in the Milk-ocean, churned by gods and Asuras. Frightened by the churning of Mandara and suspecting the arising of nectar,
the great serpents suddenly leapt up, and seeing the best of kings, terrible, they bowed and were still with their heads motionless,
like banana-groves shaken by wind at evening. Having bound with five arrows and bowstrings the (proud) one,
he bewildered the lord of Lanka, Ravana, with his army, conquered him by force, brought him under control and bound him at Mahishmati.
Hearing that Ravana, Pulastya's descendant, was bound by Arjuna, Pulastya went and himself saw Arjuna.
Requested by Pulastya, he released the Rakshasa, descendant of Pulastya. The sound of whose thousand arms' bowstring-strike
was like the thunder of a cloud at the yuga's end, bursting. Alas, the valour of the Bhargava in battle, which cut
the king's thousand arms like a golden palm-grove! Once, when asked for alms by thirsty Chitrabhanu (Agni),
the hero gave as alms to Vibhavasu the seven continents, cities, villages, cow-stations and all countries.
Chitrabhanu, desiring to consume them, blazed through all of them; by the power of that great-souled lord of men
he burned Kartavirya's mountains and forests, and the lovely, empty hermitage of Varuna's son.
Fearing the mighty Haihaya, Chitrabhanu burned it — (the hermitage of) the sage whom Varuna had earlier obtained as a splendid son,
named Vasishtha, known also as Apava. There Apava, the lord, in anger cursed Arjuna:

Because, Haihaya, you did not spare this my forest, therefore another will kill you who have done a hard deed:
brahmapuran:13:196	the mighty-armed, glorious Rama, Jamadagni's son, strong, cutting off and crushing by force your thousand arms.
brahmapuran:13:197	A Brahmin ascetic, that Bhargava, will kill you, the afflicter of enemies, for whom there was no loss of property.
Through the great king's power, he protecting subjects with dharma, thus his death came by the curse of the great sage.
Likewise the boon, Brahmins, he had himself chosen earlier. He had a hundred sons; of the great-souled one five remained,
skilled in weapons, strong, heroic, righteous, famed: Shurasena, Shura, Vrishana, Madhupadhvaja,
and Jayadhvaja by name, a great king of Avanti. Kartavirya's sons were valiant and very mighty.
Jayadhvaja's son was the mighty Talajangha; he had a hundred famed sons, remembered as the Talajanghas.
In the family of those great-souled Haihayas, best of sages, were the Vitihotras, Sujatas, Bhojas and Avantis.
The Taundikeras, famed, and Talajanghas, Bharatas and Sujatas are not named because of their numbers.
Vrisha and the others, Brahmins, were Yadavas of meritorious deeds. Vrisha was the line-holder there, and his son was Madhu.
Madhu had a hundred sons; Vrishana was the line-maker. From Vrishana all are Vrishnis, and from Madhu, Madhavas.
They are called Yadavas from Yadu's name and also Haihayas. One who here constantly recites the birth of Kartavirya would not lose wealth and would regain what was lost.
These five lineages of Yayati's sons, best of Brahmins,
of world-heroes, who support the worlds as the five elements do the moving and unmoving beings, best of sages, have been told.
Having heard the five creations, a king skilled in dharma and wealth becomes master of his five kinds of descendants and lord of them.
He obtains five hard-to-get worldly boons: long life, fame, sons, lordship and prosperity,
by holding and hearing the group of five, Brahmins. Hear now, best of sages, as I tell the line of Kroshtu.

Of the line-holder of Yadu, the sacrificer of meritorious deeds, Kroshtu: by merely hearing Kroshtu's lineage one is freed from all sins; in his line Vishnu was born, Hari, upholder of the Vrishni family.
Upamadgu, Madgu, Medura, Arimejaya, Avikshita, Akshepa, Shatrughna and Arimardana,
Dharmadhrik, Yatidharma, Dharmoksha, Andhakara, Avaha, Prativaha, and the excellent woman Sundari.
Akrura, on Ugrasena's daughter Sugatri, best of Brahmins, begot Prasena and Upadeva, radiant as gods.
Chitraka's sons were Prithu, Viprithu, Ashvagriva, Ashvabahu, Supashvaka and Gaveshana,
Arishtanemi, Ashva, Sudharma, Dharmabhrit, Subahu and Bahubahu; and the two women Shravishtha and Shravana.
On Asikni he begot Shura, Devamidhusha. On Mahishi, Shura had ten sons, on Bhojya.
Vasudeva, the mighty-armed, first called Anakadundubhi — at his birth the drums sounded in heaven.
A great uproar of drums arose in the sky, and a great rain of flowers fell at Shura's birth.
In the whole human world there was no one like him in beauty on earth; that foremost man's radiance was like the moon's.
Then Devabhaga was born, and again Devashravas; Anadhrishti, Kanavaka, Vatsavan, Grinjama,
Shyama, Shamika and Ganduusha; and his five excellent women: Prithukirti, Pritha, Shrutadeva, Shrutashrava,
and Rajadhidevi: these five were mothers of heroes. On Shrutashrava the Chaidya king Shishupala was born,
who was formerly the Daitya king Hiranyakashipu. On Prithukirti was born the son of Vriddhasharman,
the hero, lord of the Karushas, the mighty Dantavakra. Kunti made Pritha her daughter; Pandu married her,
on whom Dharma, the righteous king, was born as Yudhishthira, and likewise Bhimasena from Vayu and Dhananjaya from Indra,
the world's hero of the Pratiratha rank, of valour equal to Shakra. From Anamitra, the youngest, the delight of the Vrishnis, Shini was born.
From him the Shaineya Satyaka and Yuyudhana Satyaki; Uddhava, greatly fortunate, was the son of Devabhaga.
They declared Devashravas the best of the learned; Anadhrishti obtained a famed son, Ashmakya.
Shrutadeva bore Nivrittashatru Shatrughna. Shrutadeva's son was the renowned Naishadi,
Ekalavya, best of sages, raised by Nishadas. For the childless Vatsavan, the mighty Vasudeva Shauri gave with water-libation a heroic son, Kaushika, his own.
For the childless Ganduusha, Vishvaksena gave sons: Charudeshna, Sudeshna and Panchala Kritalakshana.
The hero who never turned back from battle, the mighty-armed Raukmineya (Pradyumna), the youngest, best of Brahmins,
whom thousands of crows followed as he went behind, saying "Today we shall feast on the charming ones slain by Charudeshna."
Tantrija and Tantripala were Kanavaka's two sons; Viru and Ashvahanu, and the two heroes Grinjima.
Shamika, son of Shyama, took the kingdom; disdaining Bhoja-hood, he obtained the Rajasuya.
Ajatashatru, destroyer of enemies, was born to him. I shall next tell of the heroic sons of Vasudeva.
Thus the threefold, many-branched, greatly mighty line of Vrishni, holding a vast lineage, is not joined with misfortunes here.
The fourteen excellent wives of Vasudeva: Pauravi, named Rohini, Madira, Adithi and Avara,
Vaishakhi, Bhadra, Sunamni the fifth, Sahadeva, Shantideva, Shridevi, Devarakshita,
Vrikadevi, Upadevi, and Devaki the seventh; Sutanu and Vadava were two female attendants.
Pauravi, named Rohini, was a daughter of Bahlika, best of sages, the eldest wife, beloved of Anakadundubhi.
She obtained as eldest son Rama, then Sharanya, Shatha, Durdama, Damana, Shubhra, Pindaraka and Ushinara.
The girl named Chitra was Rohini's daughter, nine children in all; Chitra again was famed as Subhadra, best of sages.
From Vasudeva on Devaki was born the greatly famed Shauri (Krishna); from Rama on Revati, a beloved son, Nishatha.
On Subhadra by Partha the car-warrior Abhimanyu was born; from Akrura on a Kashi girl, Satyaketu was born.
Hear all the heroic sons who were born to Vasudeva's seven fortunate wives.
Bhoja and Vijaya, both sons of Shantideva; Vrikadeva had on Sunama two sons, Gada and (another).
Vrikadevi bore the great-souled Agavaha, wife of the Trigarta king's son Shishirayana.
He made a test of manhood and did not shed manhood; (born) of dark-iron radiance in the twelfth year.
Falsely accused, Gargya, greatly agitated by anger, took a cowherd's daughter and began to have intercourse.
A cowherd apsaras, in the guise of a cowherd's wife, bore Gargya's embryo, hard to bear, unfailing.
By the command of the trident-bearer, on a mortal wife of Garga was born the mighty king named Kalayavana,
his upper half of ordinary body but with a lion's frame, a youth; the child grew up in the inner apartments of the childless king.
He became Kalayavana, best of sages, of the Yavana (king). The king, as he was fighting, asked the best of Brahmins:
Narada, the lord, told him of the Vrishni-Andhaka family; with an akshauhini of troops he then marched to Mathura.
He sent a messenger to the Vrishni-Andhaka dwelling. Then the Vrishnis and Andhakas, placing the wise Krishna in front,
gathered and took counsel out of fear of the Yavana; having made a decision, they all approved flight.
Leaving lovely Mathura, honouring Pinakin (Shiva), wishing to found Kushasthali as Dvaravati.
This is the birth of Krishna; the learned man who, pure and with controlled senses, makes it heard on parvan days becomes free of debt and happy.
